title: Trending Topics
description: Build trending topic detection with Count-Min Sketch for approximate counting, sliding time windows, burst detection algorithms, and viral content amplification detection.

segments.text: Twitter processes over five hundred million tweets per day. To find trending topics, you need to count hashtag frequencies in near real-time. Exact counting with a hash map would require terabytes of memory. Approximate counting with probabilistic data structures makes this tractable — and a five percent error is perfectly acceptable for trending.

The Count-Min Sketch uses a two-dimensional array of counters with multiple hash functions. To count a hashtag, hash it with each function and increment the corresponding counter in each row. To query, hash with each function and return the minimum counter value. It may overcount but never undercounts — perfect for trending detection.

Trending is about velocity, not total count. A hashtag used ten thousand times today isn't trending if it's used ten thousand times every day. Use a sliding time window — compare the count in the last hour to the average of the last seven days. A significant spike indicates trending. Twitter's algorithm weighs the last five minutes heavily.

Burst detection algorithms identify sudden frequency changes. The simplest: if the current rate exceeds twice the moving average, it's a burst. More sophisticated: Kleinberg's burst model uses a state automaton that transitions between normal and bursty states. The transition cost prevents false positives from random fluctuations.

A coordinated bot network creates a fake trending topic by generating fifty thousand tweets with the same hashtag in ten minutes. Your burst detector flags it as trending. How do you distinguish organic trending from manufactured trending?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you detect coordinated bot campaigns manufacturing fake trending topics?

segments.text: Hashtag indexing enables real-time search for trending content. Build an inverted index from hashtag to tweet IDs. Partition by time window — last hour, last day, last week. For the current window, use an in-memory index. For historical windows, compress and write to distributed storage. This allows both real-time trending and historical trend analysis.

Viral amplification detection tracks the spread pattern. Organic content grows gradually — ten retweets, then fifty, then two hundred. Bot-amplified content shows unnatural patterns — zero to ten thousand in five minutes with most retweets coming from accounts created in the last week. Graph analysis of the retweet network reveals these coordinated patterns.

Trending topics are location-dependent. An earthquake in Japan trends in Japan before anywhere else. Partition your Count-Min Sketches by geography — country-level and city-level. Run burst detection independently per region. This also enables the 'trending near you' feature that most social platforms offer.

The full pipeline: tweets stream through Kafka, a Flink job extracts hashtags and updates Count-Min Sketches per time window per region, burst detection runs every minute comparing current windows to historical baselines, and the results feed into a trending API that serves the mobile and web clients.
Design a trending topics system for a platform with two hundred million daily active users posting one billion items per day. Consider accuracy requirements, latency, and abuse prevention.
segments.thought_prompt: Design trending topics for 200M DAU, 1B daily posts. What data structures, pipelines, and abuse prevention?

segments.text: Trending topic detection combines probabilistic counting with burst detection. Count-Min Sketches provide memory-efficient approximate counts, sliding windows capture velocity over volume, geographic partitioning enables local trends, and viral amplification detection prevents abuse. The system is a streaming pipeline — Kafka to Flink to API — processing billions of events in near real-time.
